title: What Is a Cola in Weed? Top Colas and Premium Buds
h1: What Is a Cannabis Cola? The Top Bud, Explained
metaDescription: What is a cola on a weed plant? How top colas form, how growers shape them, hand-trimmed vs machine-trimmed flower and how to judge premium buds in the jar.
excerpt: The cola is the crown of the cannabis plant. What it is, why growers prize it and how to judge premium flower by look, smell and freshness, not size alone.
keyTakeaways: A cola is the dense bud cluster at the tip of a stem; the **main cola** crowns the plant.
Light matters more than position: studies of CBD-rich plants find the main cola isn't always the bud richest in cannabinoids.
Hand trimming can preserve more trichomes, but judge the bud, not the method.
Check trichomes, aroma, structure and the harvest date when you shop.
body:
What is a cola in weed? A cola is the long, tight cluster of buds at the tip of a stem. The main cola crowns the plant, and smaller colas form at the tips of the branches below.

Growers prize big top colas, but size alone doesn't make flower premium. Here's how colas form, how growers shape them, what trimming changes and how to judge the flower in your jar.

## What is a cola on a weed plant? The main bud site and its siblings

Botanists call a cannabis flower cluster an inflorescence. A cola is the dense, elongated stretch of flowers at the tip of a stem, where buds grow so close together that they look like one long spike.

Every plant has a main cola, also called the apical or top cola, at the end of its main stem. Each side branch can form a secondary cola of its own. Lower down, where less light reaches, buds tend to stay small and loose; shoppers know these as [popcorn buds](/blog/cannabis-popcorn-buds/).

Up close, a cola is made of many small flowers: calyxes, wispy pistils and sugar leaves, all coated in resin glands called [trichomes](/blog/cannabis-trichomes-101/). Those glands hold most of the plant's cannabinoids and aroma compounds.

## Why top colas are prized, and the limits of “bigger is better”

The top cola bud sits closest to the light, so it usually grows the biggest, densest flowers on the plant. Big, frosty colas look impressive, and growers have long seen them as the plant's prime real estate.

Research adds nuance. In a 2021 study of large, CBD-rich medical cannabis plants, the lowest buds, where little light reached, had cannabinoid levels up to 40% lower. Yet most cannabinoids were higher in the tops of side branches than in the main cola, which ran against a common industry belief. A 2023 study of high-CBD hemp found that many cultivars kept consistent cannabinoid levels from top to bottom, while others peaked in the upper canopy.

The lesson: light matters more than position, and a giant cola isn't automatically the most cannabinoid-rich part of the plant. Both studies used CBD-rich plants, so the pattern may differ in THC-rich flower. Very large, dense colas also trap moisture, so growers watch airflow and humidity closely to keep mold away.

## How growers shape colas: topping, training and canopy management

Growers can steer a plant toward one giant cola or many even ones. Common techniques include:

- **Topping.** Cutting the tip of the main stem so the plant splits into two main colas.
- **Low-stress training.** Gently bending and tying branches outward so more tips reach the light.
- **Screen of green.** Weaving branches through a net to create a flat, even canopy dotted with colas.
- **Defoliation and lollipopping.** Removing shaded leaves and lower growth so light and energy go to the top bud sites.

Each choice involves trade-offs. In the 2021 study, defoliation raised cannabinoid levels and made the plant's chemistry more even, while removing the main side branches cut flower yield sharply. Growers balance size, consistency and quality to suit their goals.

## Hand-trimmed vs. machine-trimmed flower

After harvest, buds are trimmed, either fresh or after drying, to remove the leaves around them. How that's done shows up in the jar.

| Aspect | Hand-trimmed | Machine-trimmed |
|---|---|---|
| How it's done | Trimmers work bud by bud with small scissors | Tumbling drums or blades trim large batches at once |
| Look | Natural shape, crisp edges | Often rounder, sometimes with nicks |
| Trichomes | Fewer knocked off with gentle handling | More can rub off in the machine |
| Cost | More labor, often a higher price | Faster and usually less expensive |

Neither method decides quality on its own, and some growers machine-trim first, then finish by hand. A careful machine trim of great flower can beat a sloppy hand trim of average flower, so judge the bud, not just the method.

## How to judge premium cannabis flower: trichomes, aroma, cure, structure and date

Size grabs attention, but these signs tell you more about quality:

- **Trichomes.** A heavy, sparkling coat of intact trichomes. Under a magnifier, growers look for heads that have turned cloudy rather than clear, a common sign of maturity.
- **Aroma.** A strong, distinct smell when the jar opens. Grassy or musty notes are a warning sign.
- **Cure.** Buds that feel slightly springy and sticky, not crumbly-dry or damp. A slow, careful finish after drying protects aroma and smoothness.
- **Structure and trim.** Well-formed buds, a neat trim and natural color, with no brown or gray patches.
- **Harvest date.** Fresher flower keeps more aroma, and Michigan labels list key details such as the strain and harvest date.

For a deeper walkthrough, see our [beginner's guide to buying flower](/blog/cannabis-flower-101/).

## Big buds, small buds and popcorn: is there a potency difference?

Sometimes, but less than you might think. Small buds from lower branches can test lower when they grew in shade, yet some plants show little difference from top to bottom. The THC figure on a package comes from lab testing, so it's a better guide than bud size.

Popcorn buds often cost less because they look less impressive, not necessarily because they're weaker. Shake, the loose bits that collect at the bottom of a bag or jar, works well for rolling or cooking. Our guide to [buds, shake and popcorn](/blog/cannabis-bud-vs-shake-vs-popcorn/) explains when each makes sense.

## Getting the most from premium flower

Great flower deserves a little care:

- **Grind just before you use it** to keep the aroma fresh.
- **Choose your method.** A joint is easy to share and a bowl suits quick, small sessions. A dry-herb vaporizer heats flower without burning it, which many people find brings out the flavor.
- **Use clean glass.** Resin buildup muddies the taste of even great flower.
- **Pair it well.** A favorite album, a comfortable chair and a few good snacks go a long way.

Storage protects what you paid for. Store flower in a sealed glass jar, somewhere cool and dark, away from heat and sunlight. Here's [how to store cannabis](/blog/how-to-store-marijuana/) so it stays fresh.

faq.q: What is a cola on a cannabis plant?
faq.a: It's the tight cluster of buds that forms at the tip of a stem. The main, or apical, cola sits at the peak of the main stem, and secondary colas form at the tips of the side branches. Colas are where flowers pack together most densely, which is why they produce the large, showy buds growers prize at harvest.

faq.q: Are top colas stronger than lower buds?
faq.a: Not always. Buds that grow in deep shade near the bottom of a plant can test noticeably lower. But a 2021 study of large, CBD-rich plants found most cannabinoids were higher in the tops of side branches than in the main cola, and a 2023 hemp study found little difference from top to bottom in many cultivars. The tested THC on the label is a better guide than where a bud grew.

Not automatically. Hand trimming is gentler, so buds can keep more of their natural shape and trichomes, and the trim is usually neater. Machine trimming is faster and cheaper, and a careful machine trim of good flower can still look and smoke well. Aroma, trichomes and freshness matter more than the method.

Not directly. Big and small buds from the same plant can test similarly, especially when light reaches the whole canopy. Small buds from shaded lower branches may test lower, but that comes from light, not size itself. Popcorn buds often cost less simply because they look less impressive, so check the label's THC figure instead.

faq.q: How should I store premium flower?
faq.a: Use a sealed glass jar and keep it somewhere cool and dark, away from heat, sunlight and moisture. Plastic bags can crush buds and let aroma escape. Store it where kids and pets can't reach, and open the jar only when you need to, so the aroma stays fresh.

Stack et al., Correlations among morphological and biochemical traits in high-cannabidiol hemp, Plant Direct (2023)

review.summary: 25 claims checked: 16 ok, 9 fixed (2 wrong, 4 unsupported, 3 overstated); 1 ok claims also got precision edits.

claims.claim: A cola is the dense bud cluster at a stem tip; the main (apical, top) cola crowns the main stem; side branches form secondary colas
claims.source: Danziger and Bernstein 2021 (main-stem apical inflorescence vs apical inflorescences of primary branches) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8468686/

claims.claim: Botanists call a cannabis flower cluster an inflorescence
claims.source: Danziger and Bernstein 2021 (terminology)

claims.claim: Trichomes hold most of the plant's cannabinoids and aroma compounds
claims.source: Milay et al. 2020 (glandular trichomes are where phytocannabinoids and terpenoids are made) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7593247/

claims.claim: The top cola sits closest to the light and usually grows the biggest, densest flowers
claims.source: Danziger and Bernstein 2021 (light falls off down the canopy; the industry view of the main cola)

claims.claim: 2021 study of large medical cannabis plants: lowest buds up to 40% lower; most cannabinoids higher in side-branch tops than in the main cola, against a common industry belief
claims.fix: now "large, CBD-rich medical cannabis plants" (cultivar Topaz: CBD 8-16%, THC under 1%)
claims.source: Danziger and Bernstein, Plants 2021 ("reduced considerably ... by up to 40%"; "Contrary to the common belief in the cannabis industry") https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8468686/

claims.claim: 2023 hemp study: many cultivars consistent top to bottom; others peaked in the upper canopy
claims.source: Stack et al., Plant Direct 2023 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10280002/

claims.claim: A giant cola is not automatically the most potent part of the plant; research finds the main cola is not always the most potent bud (takeaway)
claims.fix: now "most cannabinoid-rich" and "studies of CBD-rich plants", plus a line that the pattern may differ in THC-rich flower
claims.source: both studies used CBD-rich plants (Danziger and Bernstein 2021; Stack et al. 2023)

claims.claim: Large, dense colas trap moisture, so growers watch airflow and humidity to keep mold away
claims.source: PNW Plant Disease Management Handbook: high humidity and free water favor Botrytis bud blight; promote air movement; canopy management is the best prevention https://pnwhandbooks.org/plantdisease/host-disease/hemp-cannabis-sativa-gray-mold-botrytis-bud-blight-stem-canker

claims.claim: Topping, low-stress training, screen of green, defoliation and lollipopping work as described
claims.source: standard training terms; Danziger and Bernstein 2021 tested defoliation and bottom branch and leaf removal

claims.claim: 2021 study: defoliation raised cannabinoid levels in buds that gained light and evened chemistry; removing branches could cut yield sharply
claims.fix: now "removing the main side branches cut flower yield sharply"; "in buds that gained light" dropped
claims.source: Danziger and Bernstein 2021 (primary-branch removal cut inflorescence yield by up to 99%; secondary-branch removal had no significant yield effect; defoliation raised concentrations and uniformity)

claims.claim: Hand vs machine trimming table (gentler handling; more trichomes can rub off in a machine; machines faster and usually cheaper)
claims.source: hedged ("can"); no peer-reviewed comparison found, only trade press and maker-funded tests, which disagree

claims.claim: Many growers machine-trim first, then finish by hand
claims.source: no source could be opened (a trade survey summary reports operators using both methods; the article returned 403)

claims.claim: Hand-trimmed flower often keeps more trichomes (takeaway); hand-trimmed is "often" better and buds "tend to" keep more trichomes (FAQ)
claims.fix: now "can preserve more trichomes"; the FAQ answer opens "Not automatically."
claims.source: no peer-reviewed data; trade and manufacturer claims conflict

claims.claim: Under a magnifier, mature trichome heads look cloudy rather than clear
claims.fix: attributed to growers: "growers look for heads that have turned cloudy rather than clear, a common sign of maturity"
claims.source: only grower guides found; no research source

claims.claim: "Packaging date" bullet and takeaway, followed by Michigan labels listing the strain and harvest date
claims.fix: bullet and takeaway now say harvest date, the required label item
claims.source: facts/law-facts.json mi-labeling (R 420.504(1): harvest date and strain if applicable; no packaging date)

claims.claim: Michigan labels list the strain and harvest date; the THC figure on a package comes from lab testing
claims.source: facts/law-facts.json mi-labeling (testing lab, test date, THC and CBD concentration); https://www.michigan.gov/cra/-/media/Project/Websites/cra/Laws-Rules-Other-Resources/Marihuana-Rules---R-4201-to-R-4201004.pdf

claims.claim: Small buds from shaded lower branches test "somewhat" (body) or "a little" (FAQ) lower
claims.fix: both now "lower"; the study measured up to 40% lower at the bottom
claims.source: Danziger and Bernstein 2021 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8468686/

claims.claim: Popcorn buds often cost less because they look less impressive, not necessarily because they are weaker
claims.source: hedged; position effects vary by plant (Danziger and Bernstein 2021; Stack et al. 2023)

claims.claim: Grind just before use to keep the aroma; store flower in a sealed jar somewhere cool and dark
claims.source: Milay et al. 2020: "temperatures lower than -20 C and grinding of the inflorescences were the least favorable conditions"; whole inflorescences at 4 C in the dark were optimal https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7593247/

claims.claim: The freezer can make trichomes brittle (FAQ)
claims.source: Milay et al. 2020 says nothing about brittleness (it found storage below -20 C poor for terpenoids, colder than a typical home freezer)

claims.claim: A dry-herb vaporizer heats flower without burning it

review.notes: Independent fact-check: every cited study and agency page was reopened this session; Michigan law checked against facts/law-facts.json (its michigan.gov and courts.michigan.gov sources were verified by the law refuter and not refetched); High Society claims checked against facts/hs-facts.json. Writer's notes: 'cure' here means the post-harvest drying and curing of flower, not a health claim. No brand's cola product, no claim that High Society sells whole colas, no libido, sleep or pain claims.
